prompt:
A densely annotated editorial infographic plate, drawn by hand in confident ink
line with light watercolour and gouache wash on bright warm-white paper.
Contour line varies in weight and is charcoal near-black. Dimensional but not
photographic: restrained hatching, subtle texture, believable volume, selective
shadow, clean uncluttered background. Every material reads as itself — dull grey
lead, unglazed earthenware, weathered timber, damp fibrous bark — and materials
that differ in the explanation look visibly different. Quiet palette of stone,
clay, wood, and metal tones over the warm-white ground, with one or two
desaturated accents that each keep a single meaning throughout the plate.
Contemporary editorial typography: one calm display face for the title, one
highly legible face for the many small labels, sentence case, crisply printed
and correctly spelled. Annotation is dense and disciplined — leader lines,
brackets, dimension marks, magnified inset circles, small side studies — laid
out so no two leaders cross. Asymmetric composition with about a quarter of the
page left quiet. Modern printing on clean stock: fresh, crisp, and unaged. The
only lettering anywhere on the plate is the title, the deck, the labels, and the
short notes. The words hero, drawing, figure, plate, inset, zone, band, strip,
trio, column, and cutaway describe the construction of the page and are never
lettered onto it, alone or in a phrase: no headings that name parts of the
layout, no percentages or
proportions of the page, no tags in brackets after a label or note, no sentence
describing the drawing or explaining what the reader is meant to see, no
signature, monogram, date, watermark, or credit line.

The plate is headed "src", with the standing line "A desktop reference for poetry that stores words as linked entries and turns tagged definitions into clickable cross-references." beneath it.

The dominant picture, filling roughly half the page, shows A single left-to-right path. At left, a small database file drawn as a stacked slab, with a table of entries above it and a second smaller table of arrows between entries. From it, a line of raw definition text is drawn on a slip of paper, one phrase of it wrapped in a curly-braced tag. The slip enters a parser drawn as a slotted sorting block that splits the line into a short stack of segments, each segment broken again into a chain of small tokens, most plain and one marked as a reference. The chain crosses a narrow bridge into a screen at right, where the same sentence is now set as a paragraph with the tagged word underlined as a link that points back to another entry in the table at left, closing the loop.

Magnified circles set beside it show A circle on the arrow table showing one arrow leaving a source entry and arriving at a target entry, direction visible. A circle on a segment showing an indented verse and an indented quotation as distinct shapes. A circle on an entry row showing two small flags, one for a picture and one for spoken audio. A circle on the search index showing words lifted out of definitions into a lookup column.

Colour is used so that One accent for reference tokens and the links they create. A second accent for search and indexing. A third for media, meaning pictures and spoken audio. Everything else neutral.

Draw these quantities as dimension marks or counts: 3 segment types; 2 token types; 3 full-text indexes; 3 backend services; 6 screens.

These trade words appear on the plate, each set against the thing it names: items on the main table, links on the arrow table, items_fts on the search index, {word: poetry} on the tagged phrase, segments on the stack, tokens on the chain, cliches and names and literary terms on the side tables, Cmd+K on the command palette, Wails bridge on the crossing, Search and Item view and Graph view and Reports and Tables on the screens.

Letter these words onto the drawings, spelled exactly as given: raw definition text, {word: poetry}, parser, segments, tokens, reference token, Wails bridge, item page, items, links source and target, quote segment, poem segment, audio flag cliches, names, literary terms, items_fts Search, Item view, Graph view, Reports, Tables, Cmd+K Go backend, React frontend, SQLite, desktop app

Set these short notes beside what they explain: Tagged words become links to other entries; Definitions are stored as plain text, parsed on demand. Links are directed, source to target; Flags record whether picture or audio exists. Full-text indexes make keyword search fast; Separate tables hold phrases, people, terms. Graph view draws entries as nodes, links as edges; Reports list orphaned and unfinished entries. One installed application, database kept locally.
